title: How extreme rain is putting orangutans at risk
description:
Orangutans are the world’s most endangered apes and they’re now even closer to extinction. They live on two islands in southeast Asia: Sumatra and Borneo. In November, an extreme weather event in the area killed more than 1,000 people there, plus about 7% of the world’s rarest type of orangutan according to a new study.

BBC Climate and Science reporter Georgina Rannard takes us through how orangutans are being pushed towards extinction and what some countries and charities are doing to protect them.

We also hear from a conservationist making an effort to save the species.

summaryZh: 節目介紹了猩猩的現況：牠們是世界上最瀕危的大猩猩，主要分布於蘇門答臘 Sumatra 和婆羅洲 Borneo。主要威脅包括大規模砍伐以種植棕櫚油、採礦、伐木、水電工程，以及非法寵物交易和人類衝突；過去約 100 年曾有約 230,000 隻，但如今各族群數量大幅下降，婆羅洲約 104,000、蘇門答臘約 14,000、塔巴努利 Tapanuli 約 800，每年約有 2,000–3,000 隻被殺害。新研究指出去年 11 月的極端強降雨和土石流造成超過 1,000 人死亡，也殺害約 58 隻塔巴努利 Tapanuli 猩猩，約佔其總數的 7% 顯示極端天氣會把小族群推向滅絕風險。節目也說明各種保育行動，例如劃設森林保護區、繁殖與基因保護計畫，以及以國際資金補償保留森林的方案，並訪談投入救援與保育的工作者。
summaryEn: The episode explains why orangutans are closer to extinction: they live mainly on Sumatra and Borneo and face severe habitat loss from palm oil plantations, mining, logging, hydropower, illegal pet trade and human conflict. Populations have plunged—from about 230,000 a century ago to roughly 104,000 Bornean, 14,000 Sumatran and only ~800 Tapanuli orangutans, with an estimated 2,000–3,000 killed each year. A recent study found that an extreme rainfall event last November killed more than 1,000 people and about 58 Tapanuli orangutans (around 7% of that species), highlighting how extreme weather can push small populations toward extinction. The programme also covers conservation responses, including protected areas, breeding and genetic programs, and payment schemes to keep forests standing.
